title: continuous-batching-sizing-experiment-notes
summary: Working notes and small-scale experiment plan for sizing concurrency and continuous-batching windows. Includes cost impact heuristics, a light queueing model, concrete example runs, spreadsheet references and next steps for an A/B evaluation. Intended as an experiment-first complement to the playbook (not a replacement).
body:
Purpose
---
Quick, experiment-focused exploration of continuous batching + concurrency sizing with explicit cost-model ties. Goal: produce a spreadsheet-driven heuristic that SRE/infra can use to pick concurrency (num replicas / inflight requests per GPU) and batching window (max hold time) given an observed arrival pattern and desired p95 latency target.

Context and motivation
---
We know continuous batching can dramatically improve tokens/J and throughput, but naive batching increases p95 latency when arrival rates are low or bursty. This doc captures our approach to quantify the tradeoffs and produce cost-aware recommendations. This is not the canonical playbook; it's the experimental record and formulas we used to derive the numbers in the shared sheet.

High-level variables (notation)
---
- λ (lambda): observed average request arrival rate (req/s).
- s: mean tokens per request.
- B_max: maximum batch size (requests).
- T_hold: batch hold window (ms) — max time batcher will wait for more requests before dispatch.
- μ_tokens: GPU token throughput (tokens/s) for the model/quantization combo.
- S_batch = mean service tokens per batch = s * E[batch_size].
- μ_batch = μ_tokens / S_batch = effective batch service rate (batches/s).
- N: concurrency (max in-flight batches per replica).
- ρ (utilization) = λ / (N * μ_batch).

Queueing assumptions and approximations
---
- We model each replica as an M/M/N_batches style server where 'service' is processing a batch. This is an approximation (service time distribution depends on batch size), but good enough for early sizing.
- For small-to-moderate ρ (<0.8) we use a simplified tail heuristic instead of exact Erlang-C p95: p95_wait ≈ mean_wait * k_tail, where mean_wait ≈ (ρ / (1 - ρ)) * mean_service_time / N_effective and k_tail is an empirical multiplier (4–6 observed in microbench runs).
- Empirical note: service-time variance grows with batch size; larger B_max increases mean_service_time but reduces per-token cost.

Empirical calibration (summary of microbench runs)
---
- Model: llama-13b-8bit-quant (example), μ_tokens ≈ 14,000 tokens/s on p4d-ish hardware (observed).
- Typical request: s = 80 tokens avg.
- If B_max = 8 and average arrival leads to E[batch_size]=6, then S_batch ≈ 480 tokens → mean_service_time ≈ 0.034 s (≈34 ms).
- With N=2 concurrent batches, μ_batch ≈ 1 / 0.034 ≈ 29 batches/s per concurrency slot, so N*μ_batch ≈ 58 batches/s capacity.
- For arrival λ = 12 req/s, utilization ρ ≈ 12 / 58 ≈ 0.21 (comfortable). Observed p95 latency in bench: ~85 ms.
- For bursty traffic (peak short-lived λ_peak ≈ 120 req/s): if N not increased, ρ→>1 and queueing/p95 blow up. That is where autoscaling + short T_hold helps.

Cost model tie-in
---
We tie the cost to tokens processed and to number of GPUs running. Batching reduces per-token latency overhead but increases average latency per request depending on T_hold and arrival. Spreadsheet cells in the linked sheet explicitly compute: 
- tokens_per_second = λ * s
- effective_throughput_per_gpu_tokens = μ_tokens * (1 - quantization_overhead)
- GPUs_needed_flat = ceil(tokens_per_second / effective_throughput_per_gpu_tokens / efficiency_factor)
- GPU_hours = GPUs_needed * wall_time
- cost = GPU_hours * gpu_hourly_rate + networking/storage negligible for these runs
We also compute cost-per-1M-tokens for candidate (B_max, T_hold, N) knobs.

A worked example (numbers in the sheet)
---
Scenario A: steady 12 req/s, s=80 tokens, want p95 < 150 ms, minimize cost.
- Candidate knobs tried: B_max in {4,8,12}, T_hold in {5ms, 20ms, 50ms}, N in {1,2,3}.
- Best tradeoff found: B_max=8, T_hold=20ms, N=2 → p95 ~85ms, GPUs_needed=1 replica (with concurrency 2) → cost per 1M tokens = $X (see sheet).
Scenario B: bursty diurnal with λ_base=6 req/s, λ_peak=90 req/s for 30s every 5 minutes.
- Recommendation: keep low baseline concurrency (N=1) + conservative T_hold=10ms and enable burst autoscaling to add replicas quickly when queue depth > threshold. Also pre-warm concurrency in predicted windows.

Heuristics for knob selection (practical)
---
1) Start with target latency budget (p95_target). Subtract deterministic service_time (median service time for expected batch_size) to get budget for queueing/hold.
2) Pick T_hold so that when arrival rate is at at least 30–50% of capacity, expected batch size hits B_eff (empirical). A working rule: T_hold = min( max_latency_budget / 3, 30ms ).
3) Pick B_max so that per-batch service_time remains below ~120ms to avoid long tail impacts unless throughput is the primary objective.
4) Pick N to keep ρ < 0.65 under expected sustained load; use autoscale for short bursts. If stable traffic with predictable peaks, size N so ρ≈0.6 at peak.
5) When cost is primary, prefer slightly larger B_max and lower N (fewer GPUs with higher concurrency) but only if observed p95 tail remains within target in shadow runs.

What the spreadsheet does (quick tour)
---
- Input tab: arrival patterns (steady or trace upload), s distribution, model throughput, gpu price, autoscale latency for spinup.
- Batch model: computes E[batch_size] given λ and T_hold using Poisson arrivals assumption; computes mean service time per batch and variance adjustment factor.
- Queueing approximation: maps to effective utilization ρ and computes mean_wait + p95 heuristic multiplier.
- Cost tab: GPUs needed (with concurrency knobs), cost per minute/hour, cost per 1M tokens.
- Sensitivity tab: sweeps T_hold x N and produces heatmap (p95 vs cost).

Open questions / risks
---
- Tail and burst behavior: our heuristics rely on k_tail multipliers calibrated on our microbench hardware. Different hardware or model changes (longer contexts) will change k_tail substantially. Must re-calibrate for any new model family.
- Interaction with prefix/KV caching: if many requests share prefixes, effective s drops and batching dynamics change; spreadsheet has a toggle but needs validation.
- Autoscale latency: adding replicas quickly is non-trivial in private/dedicated envs; the cost model here assumes a 60–90s cold window unless warm spare replicas are kept. That cost needs explicit modeling for Dedicated customers.

Experiment plan and measurement checklist
---
1) Run steady-state microbench at λ=[2,6,12,24] req/s for s=[40,80,160], sweep B_max=[2,4,8,12], T_hold=[5,20,50] ms, N=[1,2,3]. Capture p50/p95/p99, qdepth distribution, tokens/s, GPU utilization. Record results to the linked sheet. (Owner: Aisha)
2) Run burst test: baseline λ_base=6 and repeat short bursts to λ_peak=90 for 30s, measure p95 and queue growth. (Owner: Marco)
3) Run trace-driven replay from a 24-hour production trace (anonymized). Validate model predictions vs observed metrics. (Owner: Evelyn)
4) Produce short doc (2 pages) summarizing recommended default knobs for hosted vs dedicated vs private (consider autoscale constraints). (Owner: Samir)

Decision criteria for rollout
---
- If p95 predictions are within 20% of measured p95 across validation traces and cost-per-1M-tokens improves by >8% vs current defaults, propose conservative rollout.
- Otherwise iterate on calibration and consider adding more observability hooks (per-request batch size, hold time histogram).

Next steps (concrete)
---
- Populate the sheet with microbench results this week. Link: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1aBcD_ContinuousBatchingModel (sheet name: "experiment-runs").
- Create Linear ticket ENGINF-3421 to track production rollout changes to batcher defaults and autoscale integration.
- Add per-request batch metadata to the runtime logs for 2 weeks (low-overhead sampling).

Appendix: quick Poisson-derived expected batch size formula
---
If arrivals are Poisson with rate λ and hold window T_hold, probability that k arrivals arrive in T_hold is Poisson(λT_hold). Assuming aggressive flush when B_max hit, expected batch size approximately: 
E[batch_size] ≈ sum_{n=1}^{B_max} n * P(N=n | N<=B_max) + B_max * P(N>=B_max)
where P(N=n)=e^{-λT} (λT)^n / n!. For spreadsheet we compute this numerically.

Notes to self (short):
- Watch for measurement noise at very low λ (<0.5req/s) — batching heuristics break down.
- For Dedicated customers, adjust cost model to include reserved GPU amortization and warm-standby replicas.
- Re-run calibration if we change quantization (8bit->4bit) or switch runtime kernels.
